table.text: The experimental procedure was approved by the ethics committee of the Department of Psychology, Marburg University, and conducted in accordance with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki.
All participants provided written informed consent prior to the experiment.
Three participants were excluded due to excessive eye movements (>40% of all trials) after EEG artifact rejection, resulting in 32 participants.
table.formatted: Three participants were excluded due to excessive eye movements (>40% of all trials) after EEG artifact rejection, resulting in 32 participants.

table.text: Participants were seated in front of a 22-inch Vpixx VIEWPixx monitor at a viewing distance of approximately 100 cm.

Participants were asked to report the location of the gap (faced up or down) on a target-colored Landolt-C. In 50% of trials in a block, the gaps on the two colored Landolt-C were at the same location; in the remaining trials of the block, they were at opposite locations.
Participants were instructed to respond as quickly and accurately as possible.
Prior to target match blocks, participants were informed to remember a target color to later find the colored target in the search task.
Prior to distractor match block, participants were asked to remember a distractor color to later ignore items of this color in the search task.
Participants had the chance to take a rest after finishing half of the block and the entire block.
Participants were informed that the probe displays were task-irrelevant.
Participants were asked to report the location of the gap (faced up or down) on the target-colored Landolt-C. Prior to search displays, four probe displays were presented for 50 ms every 200 ms.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Thirty-five volunteers (13 male, mean age: 22.89±3.21 years) participated in this study for payment of €10 per hour. All had normal or corrected-to-normal vision; visual acuity and colour vision were tested with the OCULUS Binoptometer 3 (OCULUS Optikgeräte GmbH, Wetzlar, Germany). All participants provided written informed consent prior to the experiment. Three participants were excluded due to excessive eye movements (>40% of all trials) after EEG artifact rejection, resulting in 32 participants. The minimum sample size of 25 was determined based on a priori power analysis (G*Power 3.1, Faul et al., 2009), with an assumed alpha of .05, power of .80, and a medium effect size (d) of .52, which was based on former studies that reported a distractor P D (e.g., Stilwell et al., 2022; van Moorselaar et al., 2023). The experimental procedure was approved by the ethics committee of the Department of Psychology, Marburg University, and conducted in accordance with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki.

table.text: As shown in Fig. 1B, the paired t test on RT revealed a significant difference between target and distractor match blocks, t(31) = -18.93, p < .001, d = 3.35, with faster RTs for target match blocks (M = 555 ms, SE = 8) than for distractor match blocks (M = 700 ms, SE = 12).

text.text: Foreknowledge of target features biases attention toward those features even before search begins, indicating pre-activation of a target template.
However, whether foreknowledge of distractor features can be similarly pre-activated remains debated.
Using EEG and a rapid serial probe presentation (RSPP) paradigm, the current study examined preparatory activation of target and distractor templates.
Task-irrelevant probes, presented before search display onset, matched the target, distractor, or were neutral in color.
Template pre-activation was indexed by a larger N2pc to templatematching probes than to neutral probes.

Results showed that target-colored probes elicited sustained and larger N2pc components than neutral probes, with this difference increasing toward the end of preparation, indicating sustained target-template pre-activation.

In contrast, distractor-colored probes elicited a reliable N2pc at the end of preparation, but this response did not differ from that elicited by neutral probes, providing no evidence for distractor template pre-activation.
During search, targetcolor foreknowledge was associated with faster responses and an earlier target N2pc, indicating more efficient target selection.
Distractor-color foreknowledge was associated with a larger distractor N2pc and no reliable distractor P D , a pattern consistent with greater attentional capture.

Overall, the findings support sustained pre-activation of the target template, but not the distractor template, during search preparation; while foreknowledge of both target and distractor features influenced attentional selection after search display onset.
Visual search is often guided by representations of target features in working memory (Carlisle, et al., 2011; Geng & Witkowski, 2019; Olivers et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2023).

text.text: Target-matching features can be prioritized before search onset, consistent with pre-activation of a target template (Grubert & Eimer, 2018 , 2020 , 2023).
text.formatted: Target-matching features can be prioritized before search onset, consistent with pre-activation of a target template <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Grubert & Eimer, 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, the use of to-be-ignored features, known as distractor templates, has been less thoroughly investigated.
Existing accounts describe how distractors are processed after search onset.

The "search and destroy" hypothesis (Moher & Egeth, 2012) proposes initial attentional capture attention followed by suppression, whereas both the "signal suppression" hypothesis (Gaspelin et al., 2025; Gaspelin & Luck, 2018; Sawaki & Luck, 2010) and the "active suppression" hypothesis (Carlisle, 2023; Zhang & Carlisle, 2023) propose that suppression without capture is possible.
text.formatted: The "search and destroy" hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Moher & Egeth, 2012)</ref> proposes initial attentional capture attention followed by suppression, whereas both the "signal suppression" hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Gaspelin et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Gaspelin & Luck, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Sawaki & Luck, 2010)</ref> and the "active suppression" hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Carlisle, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Zhang & Carlisle, 2023)</ref> propose that suppression without capture is possible.

text.text: However, pre-capture suppression does not necessarily imply pre-activation of a distractor template, and none specifies whether distractor templates can be pre-activated before search onset.

Evidence for selective pre-activation of distractor template is limited and inconclusive (Addleman & Störmer, 2022; de Vries et al., 2019; Reeder et al., 2017 Reeder et al., , 2018;; van Zoest et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Evidence for selective pre-activation of distractor template is limited and inconclusive <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Addleman & Störmer, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">de Vries et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Reeder et al., 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Reeder et al., , 2018;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">van Zoest et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Available EEG and fMRI findings have been interpreted as reflecting nonspecific control processes rather than template-specific activation (Chidharom & Carlisle, 2023; de Vries et al., 2019; Reeder et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Available EEG and fMRI findings have been interpreted as reflecting nonspecific control processes rather than template-specific activation <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Chidharom & Carlisle, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">de Vries et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Reeder et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: One reason for those mixed findings (see Arita et al., 2012; Conci et al., 2019; Zhang & Carlisle, 2023; but see Beck & Hollingworth, 2015; Becker, et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2020) may be that distractor templates are often optional because targets can be identified by another dimension.
text.formatted: One reason for those mixed findings (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Arita et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Conci et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Zhang & Carlisle, 2023</ref>; but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Beck & Hollingworth, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Becker, et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Williams et al., 2020</ref>) may be that distractor templates are often optional because targets can be identified by another dimension.

text.text: Thus, a design in which distractor information is necessary is needed to test its pre-activation.

Accordingly, the present study used distractor match blocks, in which the distractor color remained constant across trials, whereas the target color varied, together with benchmark target match blocks with the reverse arrangement.

Thus, the informed color provided the only stable feature for distinguishing target from distractor (Addleman & Störmer, 2022; Kerzel & Huynh Cong, 2022), while repeated distractor colors could promote distractor template formation (Berggren & Eimer, 2021; Stilwell et al., 2019; Wen et al., 2022).

text.text: To track template pre-activation over time, we used a rapid serial probe presentation (RSPP) task (Grubert & Eimer, 2018 , 2020 , 2023).
text.formatted: To track template pre-activation over time, we used a rapid serial probe presentation (RSPP) task <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Grubert & Eimer, 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Task-irrelevant color probes were briefly presented before search displays and either matched the informed color or a neutral color.

Previous RSPP studies showed a reliable N2pc, a posterior negativity reflecting covert deployment of attention (Hickey et al., 2009; Luck & Hillyard, 1994), to target-colored probes during preparation (Grubert & Eimer, 2018), and to distractor-colored probes when distractor colors were predictable (Grubert & Eimer, 2020).
text.formatted: Previous RSPP studies showed a reliable N2pc, a posterior negativity reflecting covert deployment of attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Hickey et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Luck & Hillyard, 1994)</ref>, to target-colored probes during preparation <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Grubert & Eimer, 2018)</ref>, and to distractor-colored probes when distractor colors were predictable <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Grubert & Eimer, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore assessed whether informed-color probes elicited a larger N2pc than neutral probes, consistent with template-specific pre-activation.

Alternatively, the distractor template might remain in an activity-silent state during preparation (e.g., Duncan et al., 2023; Lewis-Peacock et al., 2012; Rose et al., 2016; Stokes, 2015; van Moorselaar & Slagter, 2020; Wolff et al., 2017) and be reactivated by the distractor at search onset.
text.formatted: Alternatively, the distractor template might remain in an activity-silent state during preparation (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Duncan et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Lewis-Peacock et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Rose et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Stokes, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">van Moorselaar & Slagter, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Wolff et al., 2017)</ref> and be reactivated by the distractor at search onset.

text.text: Such distractor template reactivation should occur specifically in distractor match blocks, where the distractor color was the only stable informative feature.
We therefore compared search-evoked event related potentials (ERPs) between target match and distractor match blocks.

Under the "search and destroy" account, anticipated distractors should initially capture attention before being suppressed (Geng, 2014; Moher & Egeth, 2012), producing a larger distractor N2pc followed by a stronger distractor positivity (P D ) in distractor match blocks.

Finally, to assess template formation over time, we compared preparatory and search-evoked effects across block halves.
Thirty-five volunteers (13 male, mean age: 22.89±3.21 years) participated in this study for payment of €10 per hour.
All had normal or corrected-to-normal vision; visual acuity and colour vision were tested with the OCULUS Binoptometer 3 (OCULUS Optikgeräte GmbH, Wetzlar, Germany).
All participants provided written informed consent prior to the experiment.
Three participants were excluded due to excessive eye movements (>40% of all trials) after EEG artifact rejection, resulting in 32 participants.

text.text: The minimum sample size of 25 was determined based on a priori power analysis (G*Power 3.1, Faul et al., 2009), with an assumed alpha of .05, power of .80, and a medium effect size (d) of .52, which was based on former studies that reported a distractor P D (e.g., Stilwell et al., 2022; van Moorselaar et al., 2023).

text.text: The experimental procedure was approved by the ethics committee of the Department of Psychology, Marburg University, and conducted in accordance with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki.
The experiment took place in a dimly lit, electricity-shielding room.
Participants were seated in front of a 22-inch Vpixx VIEWPixx monitor at a viewing distance of approximately 100 cm.
The experiment was controlled by a Windows 7 computer (1680*1050 pixel screen resolution, 60-Hz refresh rate), using E-Prime 2.0 software.
All stimuli were presented on a black (RGB: [0,0,0]) background.
A gray fixation point (0.29° × 0.29° of visual angle; RGB: [108, 108, 108]) was presented at screen center throughout the trial and remained during the inter-trial-interval (for 1000 ms).

text.text: Each probe display included four items located 2.42° of visual angle from the screen center and evenly spaced at 45°, 135°, 225°, and 315° relative to the positive y-axis.
Each item (1.29° × 1.29° of visual angle) in the probes consisted of two closely aligned vertical and horizontal pairs of dots (0.48° × 0.48° per dot).
In each probe display, one of the items was a color singleton and the other three items were uniformly gray (RGB: [108, 108, 108]).
text.formatted: In each probe display, one of the items was a color singleton and the other three items were uniformly gray (RGB: <ref type="bibr">[108,</ref> <ref type="bibr">108,</ref> <ref type="bibr">108]</ref>).

text.text: The probe color either matched the target or the distractor color in the search display, or had a neutral color that would not appear in the subsequent search display.
Within each block, two probe colors remained constant across trials.

This probe color pair was selected from one of 12 pseudo-randomized pairs based on six colors (RGB of green [0, 142, 0]; yellow [167, 93, 0]; blue [0, 111, 234]; red [255, 0, 0]; magenta [210, 11, 213]; purple [133, 62, 252]).

text.text: One color either matched the target or distractor color, the other color served as the neutral color.
Within each trial, four probe displays were presented, two in a neutral color and two in either the target or distractor color.
The order of these displays was counterbalanced, resulting in six possible sequences.

Color and location of the colored probe item were selected independently for each probe display, with the exception that immediate location repetitions across consecutive probe displays were not allowed and that successive singletons would equally likely appear on the same or opposite sides across displays.

The search display contained six colored Landolt-C (1.62° × 1.62° of visual angle), which were presented at the 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12 o'clock positions of an imaginary clock with a radius of 4.84° from the screen center.
In each search display, two of the items were colored and the other four items were uniformly gray.
One colored Landolt-C was the target, the other the distractor; One of the two colors was constant within the block.
The other color was randomly selected from the remaining four colors and varied on a trial-by-trial basis.
Including two colored items ensured the participants must use the information provided about the target or distractor in order to perform the task.
The gaps on the gray Landolt-Cs either faced left or right, while the gaps on the colored Landolt-Cs either faced top or down.
The experiment employed a variant of rapid serial probe presentation (RSPP) paradigm (see Fig. 1A).
text.formatted: The experiment employed a variant of rapid serial probe presentation (RSPP) paradigm (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>).

text.text: Participants were asked to report the location of the gap (faced up or down) on a target-colored Landolt-C. In 50% of trials in a block, the gaps on the two colored Landolt-C were at the same location; in the remaining trials of the block, they were at opposite locations.
The search display remained on the screen until a response was made by pressing one of the two buttons using left or right index fingers.
Participants were instructed to respond as quickly and accurately as possible.
In case of an erroneous or a slow response (>1200 ms), a white text with "incorrect" or "too late" would appear for 500 ms on the screen.
text.formatted: In case of an erroneous or a slow response (>1200 ms), a white text with "incorrect" or "too late" would appear for 500 ms on the screen.

text.text: The response-to-button mapping and the hand-to-button mapping was counterbalanced across participants but was constant for each participant during the whole experiment.

Before search display onset, four consecutive task-irrelevant probe displays were presented for 50 ms every 200 ms with a blank screen in-between. each block for target match (blue) and distractor match (yellow) blocks.
Error bars indicate standard errors of the mean.
Gray dots indicate data from individual participants.
The experiment contained two block types -target match and distractor match.
Prior to target match blocks, participants were informed to remember a target color to later find the colored target in the search task.
Prior to distractor match block, participants were asked to remember a distractor color to later ignore items of this color in the search task.
Both block types contained 10 blocks with 48 trials per block, resulting in 960 trials in total.

Block sequence was randomly intermixed with the exception that repetitions of the informed color across two successive blocks were avoided to ensure that participants would not benefit from the previous block by using the same color template again.
Participants had the chance to take a rest after finishing half of the block and the entire block.
They also got feedback about mean accuracy and averaged response times after each block, lasting for 3000 ms.
Before experimental blocks, participants got familiar with the task in two steps.
In the first step, participants practiced both target match and distractor match blocks without probe displays (each with 12 trials) to ensure that they understand the search task.
In the second step, participants practiced another two blocks with the probe displays included (each with 12 trials).
Participants were informed that the probe displays were task-irrelevant.

For the analysis of response times, incorrect trials, trials where response times (RTs) exceed 2.5 SD from the conditional mean, and trials with RTs faster than 200 ms or slower than 1200 ms, were removed from the data.
To stabilize the variance, accuracy was arcsine transformed before submitting to the statistical tests.
We then conducted paired-t tests to measure the difference of RT and transformed accuracy between target and distractor match blocks.
To further investigate the role of repeated exposure, we divided each block into first and second halves.

For each dependent measure (RT and transformed accuracy), a 2×2 repeated-measures ANOVA was conducted with the factors color match (target match vs. distractor match) and block half (first vs. second), in order to assess changes over time.
The EEG was recorded with a BrainAmp amplifier from 64 Ag/AgCl active electrodes (actiCAP, Brain Products, Munich, Germany) placed according to the international 10-20 system.
Electrode impedances were kept below 5 kΩ.
The sampling rate was set at 1000 Hz (high cutoff: 250 Hz, low cutoff: 0.016 Hz) and all electrodes were online referenced to FCz.

Blinks and eye movements were monitored by deriving bipolar recordings from an electrode placed below the left eye and FP1 (vertical electrooculogram, vEOG) and from electrodes (FT9 and FT10) placed near the outer canthi of each eye (horizontal EOG, hEOG).

text.text: Processing and EEG analyses were done offline, using the FieldTrip toolbox (Oostenveld et al., 2011) and custom MATLAB scripts for preprocessing.

text.text: EEG was re-referenced to the average of the left and right mastoid, and bandpass-filtered between 1 and 35 Hz.
Next, the continuous EEG was segmented into 1300 ms trials ranging from 100 ms before the first probe display to 400 ms after the search display.

Trials with poor behavioral performance (incorrect responses and RT outside 2.5 SD of the mean), large eye blinks (with vEOG exceeding ±80 μV), or horizontal eye movements (with hEOG exceeding ±50 μV) were excluded from further analysis.
We focused the analysis of probeand search-related potentials on electrodes PO7/8, based on previous studies using the RSPP paradigm (Grubert & Eimer, 2018 , 2020 , 2023).

text.text: To this end, we automatically rejected trials with electrodes PO7/8 amplitudes outside ±80 μV.
On average, this result in 19.65% (SE =1.45) of all trials being rejected across the 32 qualified participants.

The remaining trials were further segmented into 500 ms time windows time-locked to every probe displays (-100 to 400 ms) and 800 ms time windows time-locked to search displays (-200 to 600 ms), followed by 100 ms pre-probe and 200 ms pre-search baseline corrections, respectively.

For probe-evoked potentials, ERPs measured at electrodes PO7/8 were separately averaged for each probe time (probe 1-4), probe color (target/distractor color vs. neutral color), and laterality (contralateral vs. ipsilateral to the side of singleton probe).

For search-evoked potentials, ERPs measured at electrodes PO7/8 were separately averaged for color match (target match vs. distractor match) and laterality (contralateral vs. ipsilateral to the side of target/distractor).

N2pc components to probes were quantified based on mean amplitudes of difference waveforms (contralateral minus ipsilateral to the side of the singleton probe) within an 80 ms time window starting at 180 ms after probe display onset.
The start of this time window was determined by measuring the time point when the grand-averaged probe N2pc (pooled across all probes and blocks) reached 50% of the peak amplitude (at -0.18 μV).
This method is analogous to previous studies that used similar probe presentation procedures (Grubert & Eimer, 2018 , 2020 , 2023).

text.text: For target and distractor match blocks, the N2pc modulation for probes across different probe times was separately assessed with 2×2×4 repeated-measures ANOVA with the factors laterality (contralateral vs.
ipsilateral to the side of the singleton probe), probe color (target/distractor color vs. neutral color) and probe time (probe 1-4).

Whenever this analysis revealed a significant interaction between laterality and probe time, planned contrasts were considered to reveal a potential difference between contralateral and ipsilateral ERPs for individual probes.

For ERPs time-locked to the search displays, an early positivity was defined from 120-200 ms based on previous studies (Corriveau et al., 2012; Oxner et al., 2024; Sawaki & Luck, 2010), no other positivity was observed.

text.text: This time window largely overlaps with that of the Ppc component, which reflects salience-driven encoding (Fortier-Gauthier et al., 2012), as well as the P D component, which indexes distractor inhibition (Gaspar et al., 2016; Hickey et al., 2009).

text.text: Because both components can be modulated by attention, differences in distractor-elicited positivity between target match and distractor match blocks alone cannot unambiguously distinguish between these two processes.
To address this issue, we included target-elicited positivity as a control condition.

Specifically, lateralized amplitudes (calculated by subtracting ipsilateral from contralateral waveforms) within the 120-200 ms interval were submitted to a 2×2 repeated-measures ANOVA with the factors color match (target match vs. distractor match), and lateral role (lateral target vs. lateral distractor).

If the early positivity primarily reflects salience-driven encoding (i.e., the Ppc), we would expect a main effect of lateral role, with larger positivities elicited by both lateral targets and by lateral distractors, regardless of the instructed task.

By contrast, if the early positivity predominantly reflects distractor inhibition (i.e., the P D ), we would expect enhanced distractor-elicited positivity in distractor match blocks relative to target match blocks, reflected in a significant interaction between color match and lateral role.
The N2pc was analyzed in the time window of 220-300 ms post-stimulus, following the conventional time range reported in prior literature (Eimer, 1996; Henare et al., 2024; Luck & Hillyard, 1994).

The presence of lateralized ERPs was further assessed by conducting onesample t tests against zero (two tailed p < .05).

text.text: Previous studies have found that repeated distractor exposure can reduce distractor P D amplitudes, which has been interpreted as reflecting a reduced need for distractor inhibition (Hanne et al., 2025; van Moorselaar et al., 2020; van Moorselaar & Slagter, 2019; Wang & Theeuwes, 2018).

text.text: To examine whether repeated exposure to a distractor color similarly modulated attentional selection before search display appears, we compared probe-elicited N2pc components between the first and second halves of trials across all blocks.

If repeated exposure reduces the attentional selection of the distractor-matching feature, the N2pc elicited by probes matching distractor color was expected to be less negative in the second half of blocks.
Indeed, N2pc amplitudes were numerically smaller in the second than in the first half of blocks.

This difference reached significance only at probe 4, whereas the difference at probe 1 was marginal (Fig. 5A; probe 1: M diff = 0.22 μV, SE= 0.11, t(31) = 2.01, p = .053; probe 2: M diff = 0.09 μV, SE = 0.13, t(31) = 0.69, p = .493; probe 3: M diff = -0.03 μV, SE = 0.15, t(31) = -0.20, p = .843; probe 4: M diff = 0.23 μV, SE = 0.10, t(31) = 2.31, p = .028, d = 0.41).

text.text: Control analyses of neutral probes in distractor match blocks did not reveal significant N2pc attenuation across block halves.
Critically, the experience-related changes for distractor-colored probes did not differ significantly from those observed for neutral probes at either probe 1 or probe 4 (both ps >.050).

text.text: The observed reductions therefore cannot be attributed specifically to distractor-template processing.
Exploratory analysis: Attenuated attention to the distractor feature during preparation predicts less attentional capture during search

Previous studies have also suggested that preparatory attentional processes prior to search display onset can influence subsequent distractor handling during visual search (van Zoest et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Previous studies have also suggested that preparatory attentional processes prior to search display onset can influence subsequent distractor handling during visual search <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(van Zoest et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Zhao et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Building on this notion, we examined whether experience-related changes in preparatory activity would predict adjustments in distractor processing once the search display appeared.
Specifically, we focused on the last probe of each trial, which was assumed to reflect the preparatory state immediately before search onset.

The N2pc amplitudes elicited by distractor-colored probes were therefore used to predict the corresponding N2pc modulation in the search task (i.e., the distractor N2pc observed within 320-400 ms in distractor match blocks).

As shown in Fig. 5B, changes in the N2pc (2nd half minus 1st half), elicited by the distractor-colored probe, were positively correlated with changes in the distractor N2pc (320-400 ms) during search (r = .46, p = .008).
text.formatted: As shown in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">5B</ref>, changes in the N2pc (2nd half minus 1st half), elicited by the distractor-colored probe, were positively correlated with changes in the distractor N2pc (320-400 ms) during search (r = .46, p = .008).

text.text: This association suggests that attenuated preparatory attention to the distractor feature was linked to smaller attentional capture by the distractor feature during search.
In contrast, changes in the target-colored probe N2pc were unrelated to target N2pc modulations (r = -.24, p = .180).
Together, these results indicate that experience-related adjustments in preparatory attention, particularly toward distractor features, shaped subsequent attention selection in visual search.
The present study examined whether and when distractor templates are pre-activated before search onset, and whether their use changes with repeated exposure.
Target-colored probes elicited a larger N2pc than neutral probes throughout preparation, consistent with sustained pre-activation of target templates.

In contrast, distractor-colored probes elicited a reliable N2pc only late in preparation, but this did not differ from responses to neutral probes, providing no evidence for distractor template preactivation.
Block-half changes were likewise not distractor-specific.

During search, the target triggered an earlier N2pc in target match blocks than distractor match blocks, suggesting that foreknowledge of the target feature enhanced the efficiency of target selection.

By comparison, the distractor in general triggered a more pronounced N2pc in distractor match blocks compared to target match blocks, indicating greater attentional capture when distractor identity was known beforehand.
Is there pre-activation of distractor templates during preparation?
Neural evidence for distractor template pre-activation remains mixed.

Spatial-cueing studies have sometimes reported increased alpha power contralateral to expected distractor locations, consistent with inhibitory preparation (Duncan et al., 2025; van Zoest et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2023), whereas others found no such effects (Duncan et al., 2023; Ferrante et al., 2023; Noonan et al., 2016; van Moorselaar et al., 2020; van Moorselaar & Slagter, 2019).

text.text: In the feature domain, increased posterior alpha power following negative cues has been interpreted as general inhibition rather than distractor-specific template activation (de Vries et al., 2019; Reeder et al., 2017 Reeder et al., , 2018;; van Zoest et al., 2021).

text.text: Thus, direct neural evidence for distractor template pre-activation remains limited.
The present RSPP addressed this issue by comparing N2pc components elicited by task-irrelevant probes that either matched the distractor color or a neutral color.
In distractor match blocks, the distractor color was the only constant informative color across trials, making its use necessary.
Although distractor-colored probes elicited a robust N2pc at the final probe, this response did not differ from that to neutral probes and was therefore not distractor-specific.
Instead, the late N2pcmay reflect a general increase in probe-elicited attentional selection as search onset approached.
Because the number of probes was fixed, the final probe may signal imminent search onset, making temporal expectation a plausible explanation.
This speculation is compatible with evidence that the timing of N2pc for target-colored probes varies with the expected search onset (Grubert & Eimer, 2018).
text.formatted: This speculation is compatible with evidence that the timing of N2pc for target-colored probes varies with the expected search onset <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Grubert & Eimer, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: N2pc responses to distractor-colored probes were reduced across block halves, particularly at the final probe.

Similar reductions following learned distractor regularities have been linked to decreased need for distractor inhibition after search onset, as indexed by reduced P D amplitudes (Hanne et al., 2025; van Moorselaar et al., 2020; van Moorselaar & Slagter, 2019; Wang & Theeuwes, 2018).
text.formatted: Similar reductions following learned distractor regularities have been linked to decreased need for distractor inhibition after search onset, as indexed by reduced P D amplitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Hanne et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">van Moorselaar et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">van Moorselaar & Slagter, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Wang & Theeuwes, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, our effects concerned preparatory probe-elicited N2pc rather than post-display Pᴅ.
More critically, the present changes did not differ between distractor-colored and neutral probes.

Therefore, they cannot be attributed specifically to distractor template learning and may instead reflect more general repetition-related processes, such as reduced responsiveness to task-irrelevant probes.
Overall, we thus found no convincing evidence for distractor template pre-activation.

Former research has shown that a salient distractor can elicit an early positivity, often appearing before or overlapping with the N2pc time window (e.g., Gaspar & McDonald, 2014; Sawaki & Luck, 2010).

text.text: This distractor positivity (i.e., early P D ) has sometimes been interpreted as an index of active suppression, with larger positivities reflecting more efficient suppression (Feldmann-Wüstefeld & Vogel, 2019; Gaspelin et al., 2023; Gaspelin & Luck, 2018).

text.text: We observed an early distractor positivity (120-200 ms) in both target match and distractor match blocks.

Although positivity was larger in distractor match blocks, this effect did not interact with display layout, indicating that the early positivity was not specifically tied to the instructed distractor color.

The response therefore provides little evidence for template-specific suppression and is more consistent with a general salience-driven encoding response, such as the Ppc (Barras & Kerzel, 2016; Corriveau et al., 2012; Fortier-Gauthier et al., 2012; Jannati et al., 2013; McDonald et al., 2023), although an overlapping inhibitory contribution cannot be excluded.

text.text: In the later time window (220-400 ms), distractors elicited a larger N2pc in distractor match than target match blocks.

This pattern is consistent with the reactivation account proposed in the introduction, in which a distractor representation may remain activity-silent during preparation and be reactivated when a matching distractor appears.
The distractor acts as a retrieval cue that increases attentional selection.
However, this possible reactivation did not support any forms of suppression.
Specifically, if suppression had been exclusively engaged, the distractor N2pc should have been absent in distractor match blocks.

Alternatively, if the template had supported a "search and destroy" (Moher & Egeth, 2012) account, the enhanced N2pc should have been followed by a stronger P D , reflecting a later suppression (i.e., late P D ) following capture.
text.formatted: Alternatively, if the template had supported a "search and destroy" <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Moher & Egeth, 2012)</ref> account, the enhanced N2pc should have been followed by a stronger P D , reflecting a later suppression (i.e., late P D ) following capture.

text.text: Neither pattern was observed.
Instead, distractor foreknowledge was associated with a larger distractor N2pc without a subsequent P D .
Thus, the findings provide little support for either "suppression only" or "search and destroy" accounts.
Taken together, distractor foreknowledge appeared to alter attentional selection only after search onset, and increasing rather than preventing capture by the anticipated distractor.

Behavioral performance was substantially better when participants knew the target color than when they knew the distractor color, consistent with previous work showing an advantage of positive over negative cues (Arita et al., 2012; Carlisle, 2023; Conci et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022; Zhang & Carlisle, 2023).

text.text: In line with these findings, an earlier target N2pc was observed for target match blocks (220-300 ms) than for distractor match blocks (320-400 ms), which is also consistent with previous reports of faster or larger target N2pc following positive than negative cues (Berggren & Eimer, 2021; Carlisle & Nitka, 2019; Salahub & Emrich, 2021).

text.text: The use of distractor information may be less efficient because they require additional interpretation and executive control before guiding attention (Chidharom & Carlisle, 2023; de Vries et al., 2019; Rajsic et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020; Zhang & Carlisle, 2023).

text.text: The N2pc responses to preparatory probes further demonstrate a difference between foreknowledge of target and distractor information.
Target-colored probes triggered a larger N2pc than distractorcolored probes, suggesting that the color information was used selectively.
This selectivity also argues against nonspecific feature-priming, which should affect both informed colors similarly.

In addition, target-colored probes triggered a larger N2pc than neutral probes starting from the first probe onward, whereas distractor-colored probes, triggered an N2pc only at the final probe and did not differ from neutral probes.
Thus, target but not distractor information showed clear evidence of sustained template-specific pre-activation.

Notably, this sustained target-template pre-activation differs from Grubert and Eimer (2018 , 2020 , 2023) who found N2pc elicited by target-colored probes only shortly before search onset, suggesting more transient mode of pre-activation.
text.formatted: Notably, this sustained target-template pre-activation differs from <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Grubert and Eimer (2018</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">, 2023)</ref> who found N2pc elicited by target-colored probes only shortly before search onset, suggesting more transient mode of pre-activation.

text.text: This discrepancy might be due to different settings of the stimulus-onset asynchrony (SOA) between two subsequent search displays.

Their fixed inter-search SOA caused early probes to follow the preceding search almost immediately (i.e., 50 ms), potentially overlapping with decision and response processes, therefore participants might not have been ready for the next trial's template pre-activation at first few probes.
In our study, the next trial began only after a response had been made, which may have allowed the template preparation to begin earlier.

However, target template pre-activation may still be strategically timed, as Grubert and Eimer (2018) showed that the N2pc elicited by target-colored probes was delayed when search onset was expected later.
text.formatted: However, target template pre-activation may still be strategically timed, as <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Grubert and Eimer (2018)</ref> showed that the N2pc elicited by target-colored probes was delayed when search onset was expected later.

text.text: Thus, temporal expectations may regulate when target templates become active.
The present findings demonstrate that repeated exposure also influenced search efficiency.
Behaviorally, responses became faster across block halves, particularly in distractor match blocks, suggest that participants became more efficient as the distractor color repeated.
At the neural level, greater reductions in the N2pc elicited by distractor-colored probes was associated with an attenuated distractor N2pc during search.
Thus, reduced preparatory attention to distractor features predicted less later capture.
No comparable relationship emerged for target templates, possibly because targetbased selection was already efficient and therefore less susceptible to experience-related improvement.

These findings also align with the contingent capture framework (Folk et al., 1992; Folk & Remington, 1998), according to which attentional capture depends on whether a stimulus matches the current attentional set.
text.formatted: These findings also align with the contingent capture framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Folk et al., 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Folk & Remington, 1998)</ref>, according to which attentional capture depends on whether a stimulus matches the current attentional set.

text.text: Such contingencies can themselves be shaped by experience and repetition (Chelazzi et al., 2019; van Zoest et al., 2021; Vatterott & Vecera, 2012).
text.formatted: Such contingencies can themselves be shaped by experience and repetition <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chelazzi et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">van Zoest et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Vatterott & Vecera, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Our results extend this account by demonstrating that preparatory attentional responses to distractor features can be adaptively tuned with experience to reduce unwanted distractor capture during search.
In conclusion, the present study provides no convincing evidence that distractor templates are preactivated during preparation.
Nevertheless, distractor foreknowledge influenced attentional selection after search display onset.
And this influence may be adjusted through experience-dependent changes in attentional processing.
